hooks.command: c=$(jq -r ".tool_input.command // empty"); case "$c" in *--no-index*) printf '%s\n' 'blocked: --no-index makes git read a path as a plain file, so it prints any file on disk -- cosign.key, a .env, a credential outside this repo -- past the Read deny rules in .claude/settings.json. Describe such a file with ls -l or wc -c instead.' >&2; exit 2;; esac; exit 0

f=$(jq -r ".tool_input.file_path // empty"); case "$f" in *.sh) command -v shellcheck >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0; out=$(cd "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR" 2>/dev/null || exit 0; shellcheck -x "$f" 2>&1) || { printf "%s\n" "$out" >&2; exit 2; };; esac; exit 0

_note_podman_ps: `podman ps` is allowed with the mutating `--sync` form knowingly included. `--sync` forces Podman's stored state to be rebuilt from what the OCI runtime reports, so it is a write, not a read. It is allowed anyway: it reconciles bookkeeping with ground truth and cannot create, start, stop or delete a container or image, and the destructive podman verbs are gated separately under `ask` and `deny`. There is no narrower rule that helps -- permission patterns match by prefix and flags may appear in any order, so `Bash(podman ps -a:*)` would admit `podman ps -a --sync` just as readily. The choice is therefore between allowing this form and prompting on every `podman ps`, and the read is far more common. Raised by chatgpt-codex-connector on #93 and verified against podman 5.8.4's man page.
_note_run_tests: `./tests/run-tests.sh` is the one allow rule here that names a repository path, and allowing a script is allowing whatever that script runs: the rules in this table gate the Bash tool's argv, not what an approved command then executes. So the runner's argument handling is part of this boundary. It resolves a selection argument to a `test-*.sh` inside `tests/` and refuses anything else; before that it ran any readable path, which made `./tests/run-tests.sh /tmp/payload` a way to execute arbitrary code with no prompt and reach past every `ask` and `deny` rule beside it -- `cosign sign`, `git push --force`, `Read(./cosign.key)`. What is left is bounded by that directory: a file written at `tests/test-*.sh` is run by the next suite run, exactly as one written for the no-argument glob is, and that is the surface shellcheck and tests/test-shell-syntax.sh already cover. A symlink in `tests/` still points wherever it points, but placing one takes a command this table gates. tests/test-harness.sh and tests/test-claude-settings.sh hold the runner to this by executing it.
_note_git_diff: `git diff` is allowed, and `git diff --no-index` compares two paths as plain files rather than as repository content -- so it reads and prints any file this uid can open, untracked, gitignored or outside the repo. That is what the `Read(./cosign.key)`, `Read(./.env)` and `Read(./.env.*)` rules below exist to stop, and they do not reach it: those gate the Read tool, and this is the Bash tool. No permission rule closes it either. Patterns match by prefix and flags may appear in any order, so a narrower allow such as `Bash(git diff --stat:*)` admits `git diff --stat --no-index` exactly as `_note_podman_ps` describes for `podman ps --sync`, and a `Bash(git diff --no-index:*)` deny matches that one ordering and misses the same command with a flag in front of it. Moving `git diff` to `ask` would prompt on the most common read here. So the PreToolUse hook above blocks the flag instead: a hook sees the whole command string, not a prefix. `--no-index` has no abbreviated spelling -- `--no-inde` and shorter do not trigger it -- so matching the literal matches the flag. Residual, stated rather than implied: a hook keyed on a string is defeated by a command that does not contain the string, and nothing bounds what a command reads once it has started. This re-gates the one pre-approved command that reaches past the deny list; it is not a sandbox. tests/test-claude-settings.sh holds both halves to this by executing them.
_note_gh_api: gh api is intentionally in `ask`, never `allow`. Permission rules match by command prefix, and `gh api` switches to POST as soon as -f/-F is present and honours -X for any method. An allow rule such as Bash(gh api repos/:*) would therefore approve mutations, including the workflow-dispatch endpoint that `gh workflow run` is listed under `ask` to gate.
